cards.front: One pass keeps the running sum left of a[0] through a[i]. How do you get the sum after index i without a second loop?
cards.finding: No card says the other side of a split is the total minus the running sum. After the theory he invented a two-ended balance for find-the-pivot-integer and needed a submission to debug its step rule; before it he built a second array or re-summed slices.

cards.front: An n-element array is cut into a non-empty left part and a non-empty right part. Which indexes i can end the left part?
cards.finding: count-partitions-with-even-sum-difference looped to i < n and counted a split with an empty right side. The deck's off-by-one cards cover the end of a range, not the number of cut points.

cards.front: Many ranges [s, e], ends included, each cover points s through e. How does one prefix-sum pass count the cover of every point?
cards.finding: The unit files points-that-intersect-with-cars under prefix sums, but no card links ranges to a prefix sum; the inverse card stops at recovering x. The solve took 18 active minutes and ended as a Set of points. This card supplies the planned method; the edited range-end card is what fixes his actual off-by-one.

cards.front: A problem sums every odd-length subarray. In how many odd-length subarrays of an n-element array does a[i] appear?
cards.finding: He had the contribution idea before the theory but reached the count by trial on the judge: 3 wrong answers, the last one missing the division by 2. The only contribution card counts prefix sums (n - i), not subarrays through an index.

cards.front: A loop will push numbers into a result array that starts with one value v. How do you declare the array in TypeScript?
cards.finding: running-sum-of-1d-array had the right algorithm and lost its one-shot to exactly this declaration. Six of ten problems, two of the three post-theory ones, had a compile error (8 in total) and no card covers TypeScript declarations. The other seven compile errors' code is not in the data, so only this problem is listed.

cards.front: A single pass builds running totals of values that may be negative. How do you calculate prefix sum y[i] from the previous prefix sum?
cards.finding: The single-pass idea held: both post-theory sum problems keep one running total. Its positive-only examples left the sign open, and ant-on-the-boundary subtracted a negative step, so the rewrite adds that case.

cards.front: A range runs from l through r, r included. Which end do you write in pre[...], slice(l, ...) and a loop test?
cards.finding: He passed its review, then wrote j < end for an included end in points-that-intersect-with-cars: the rule was tied to pre[] and did not transfer. The rewrite states it for the three forms his code takes: pre, slice and a loop test.

cards.front: A problem needs the largest value of a[0..i] for every i. How do you get them all in one pass?
cards.finding: Its example is a running product, which no problem of the unit needs; smallest-stable-index-i needs a running maximum and a suffix minimum, which he computed per index with Math.max(...slice) before the theory. Not tested post-theory; the rewrite aims it at that case.

cards.front: A problem asks how many values are smaller than each value. What does the prefix sum of a histogram of key frequencies give?
cards.finding: Recited without a miss and used by no solve; the range card covers it.

cards.front: A problem asks for the running total at every position. What is the prefix sum of a sequence of numbers?
cards.finding: He wrote a correct running-total array before the theory (running-sum-of-1d-array), so it confirmed more than it taught. After it, both sum problems were written as running totals; their failures were elsewhere.
